content: Macrolide antibiotics are among the most frequently prescribed antibiotics globally and are used to treat a wide variety of infections. However, their use is associated with an increased risk of adverse events. Observational studies have been the primary source of information on these adverse events, but such studies are prone to bias, as it is often difficult to differentiate between events caused by the antibiotics themselves and those caused by the underlying diseases being treated. Since adverse events are specific to the treatment rather than the disease, combining data from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) across different diseases allows for a more robust analysis of these events. The objective of this study was to quantify the incidence of adverse events in individuals taking macrolide antibiotics compared to those taking a placebo, regardless of the indication for treatment. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, LILACS, and Web of Science, up to May 2018. They also reviewed clinical trial registries and reference lists of relevant studies. The inclusion criteria were RCTs comparing macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin, or roxithromycin) to placebo, with macrolides administered via any route. Concomitant medications were allowed if equally available to both groups. Data collection and analysis were performed independently by two reviewers. The risk of bias in the included studies and the quality of evidence for each outcome were assessed. Adverse events, deaths, and the development of macrolide-resistant bacteria were analyzed separately. Specific adverse events occurring in at least 5% of participants in any group were reported, and meta-analyses were conducted when three or more studies reported the same adverse event. A total of 183 studies involving 252,886 participants were included. The indications for macrolide use varied widely, with most studies focusing on acute respiratory tract infections, cardiovascular diseases, chronic respiratory diseases, gastrointestinal conditions, or urogenital problems. The majority of trials were conducted in secondary care settings, and azithromycin and erythromycin were the most commonly studied macrolides. Most studies (89%) reported some adverse events or explicitly stated that none were observed. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most frequently reported. Compared to placebo, macrolides were associated with higher rates of diarrhea (odds ratio [OR] 1.70, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.34 to 2.16; low-quality evidence), abdominal pain (OR 1.66, 95% CI 1.22 to 2.26; low-quality evidence), and nausea (OR 1.61, 95% CI 1.37 to 1.90; moderate-quality evidence). Vomiting (OR 1.27, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.56; moderate-quality evidence) and unspecified gastrointestinal disorders (OR 2.16, 95% CI 1.56 to 3.00; moderate-quality evidence) were also more common in participants taking macrolides. The absolute risk increase for these adverse events was as follows: 85 per 1000 for unspecified gastrointestinal disorders, 72 per 1000 for diarrhea, 62 per 1000 for abdominal pain, 47 per 1000 for nausea, and 23 per 1000 for vomiting. The number needed to treat for an additional harmful outcome (NNTH) ranged from 12 for unspecified gastrointestinal disorders to 45 for vomiting. There was no consistent difference in gastrointestinal adverse events between different macrolides or routes of administration. Taste disturbances were more frequently reported in participants taking macrolides, although the confidence intervals were wide, and there was moderate heterogeneity (OR 4.95, 95% CI 1.64 to 14.93; low-quality evidence). Hearing loss was also more common in participants taking macrolides compared to placebo, but this outcome was reported in only four studies (OR 1.30, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.70; low-quality evidence). No evidence was found to suggest that macrolides caused more cardiac disorders (OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.40; very low-quality evidence), hepatobiliary disorders (OR 1.04, 95% CI 0.27 to 4.09; very low-quality evidence), or changes in liver enzymes (OR 1.56, 95% CI 0.73 to 3.37; very low-quality evidence) compared to placebo. Similarly, there was no evidence that macrolides increased the incidence of appetite loss, dizziness, headache, respiratory symptoms, blood infections, skin and soft tissue infections, itching, or rashes. Interestingly, macrolides were associated with lower rates of cough (OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.80; moderate-quality evidence) and respiratory tract infections (OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.80; moderate-quality evidence) compared to placebo, likely reflecting their therapeutic effects rather than adverse events. Participants taking macrolides also reported less fever (OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.00; moderate-quality evidence), although this finding was not statistically significant. There was no increase in mortality among participants taking macrolides compared to placebo (OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.06; low-quality evidence). Only 24 studies (13%) provided data on macrolide-resistant bacteria. Resistance was more commonly identified immediately after exposure to macrolides, but the differences in resistance over time were inconsistent. Pharmaceutical companies supplied the trial medication or funding, or both, for 91 of the included trials. In conclusion, macrolides as a class significantly increase the risk of gastrointestinal adverse events. However, many trials did not clearly report adverse events as outcomes, describe the methods used to elicit adverse events, or provide detailed data on the number of participants experiencing adverse events in both the intervention and placebo groups. This lack of detailed reporting was particularly evident for the adverse event of bacterial resistance.
